items.what: Lojban uses different connective forms for joining arguments, predicates and whole clauses (.e / je / gi'e / .ije) precisely so that 'and' never leaves open what is being joined; the spec uses one AND for units and for clauses, and both begin with a bare root.
items.example: mi dunda le cukta gi'e lebna lo rupnu (clause-and) vs lo palku .e lo mapku (argument-and)
items.how_now: CLAIM eat AGENT A THEME bread AND drink . -- 'A eats bread and drink' (unit AND unit) or 'A eats bread and A drinks' (clause AND clause)? Same with ... THEME B AND run AGENT C .
items.suggestion: Rule: AND/OR/BUT between clauses must have the clauses in ( ), or add one distinct clause-level joiner; keep bare AND/OR for units only. Then have the validator reject a second occurrence of a role after AND.

items.what: Every Lojban predicate has a dictionary-defined place structure, so which participant goes where is never a writer's choice; the spec's tagged roles avoid Lojban's memorised numbered places (its main usability cost) but nothing fixes which roles a given root takes.
items.example: tavla: x1 talks to x2 about x3 in language x4; klama: goer, destination, origin, route, vehicle
items.how_now: fear AGENT A THEME dog / fear THEME A CAUSE dog / (afraid) THEME A ABOUT dog -- all legal, no rule picks one
items.suggestion: Copy the dictionary idea, not the numbering: each lexicon entry lists its role frame (e.g. fear: AGENT = feeler, THEME = thing feared) and validate.py warns on roles outside the frame.

items.category: what a root means as a head
items.what: In Lojban a predicate word used as an argument always refers to its first place (lo klama = a goer), and the event or the proposition needs an explicit abstractor (nu, du'u); the spec says only 'position decides its use'.
items.example: lo klama 'goer' vs lo nu klama 'a going' vs lo se klama 'destination'
items.how_now: CAUSE fail -- the failure (event)? the failing thing? ; THEME big -- bigness, or a big thing? ; AGENT teach -- teacher or teaching?
items.suggestion: Rule: a root as head names the thing the root is true of as THEME (big = a big thing, fail = a failing thing); the event or fact is always a block { fail THEME x }; a property or amount is root + OF (size OF x). State it once in Clarifications.

items.what: Lojban distinguishes inclusive or, exclusive or, if-and-only-if, only-if and whether-or-not as separate connectives; the spec has OR and IF and does not say which OR is meant.
items.example: .a 'and/or', .onai 'either, not both', .o 'iff', na.a 'only if', .u 'whether or not'
items.how_now: A OR B (reading unstated); iff = two IF sentences; only-if = IF { NOT B } { NOT A }; whether-or-not = DESPITE { B OR NOT B }
items.suggestion: Rule: OR is inclusive except directly under ASK. Add one particle in the connective slot for 'exactly one of' (or write EXACT 1 OF (A OR B) and bless it). Bless IF with ONLY in front of the condition block for 'only if', and both directions for iff, as the single approved forms.

items.what: A non-logical connective pairs the members of two lists in order (fa'u), distinct from plain 'and' and from the joint/mass 'and' (joi).
items.example: lo lanme fa'u lo guzme cu danlu fa'u spati 'sheep and melons are animals and plants respectively'
items.how_now: cannot in one clause; two clauses: (animal) THEME sheep AND (plant) THEME melon (joint reading is covered by WHOLE (A AND B))
items.suggestion: Leave out of the particle list; rule that paired lists are written as separate clauses or as EACH over a NOTE list. Mention it so writers do not try AND ... AND and get the cross-product reading.

items.what: Lojban counts how many times an event happens (number + roi), which time it is (number + re'u, 'for the first time') as part of the tense slot; the spec has only vague frequency particles (OFTEN, RARE, AGAIN).
items.example: paroi 'once', reroi 'twice', pare'u 'for the first time'
items.how_now: PAST run AGENT ME THEME test SPAN 3 time ? (SPAN is duration/extent, so this is a guess); 'for the first time' and 'every 5 minutes / twice a day' have no home
items.suggestion: Let a number or ORD n stand in the aspect slot before a new particle TIMES (3 TIMES, ORD 1 TIMES, WHAT TIMES), and rule that a rate is TIMES plus a SPAN phrase (2 TIMES SPAN 1 day).

items.what: A tense can be set once (ki) and holds for following sentences until reset, so narrative does not repeat the tense on every clause.
items.example: mi pu ki fengu binxo .i le nixli cu klaku cfari '(earlier) I got angry. The girl started crying.'
items.how_now: STORY PAST ... . STORY PAST ... . STORY PAST ... . (PAST repeated on every sentence, since unmarked = timeless)
items.suggestion: Rule: a time particle placed in the header right after the opener (before relations) sets the default time for following sentences with the same opener until another header time appears; cheap for the decoder and removes most PAST tokens in stories and reports.

items.what: Lojban separates innate capability (ka'e), capability never yet exercised (nu'o), demonstrated capability (pu'i) and actual occurrence (ca'a); the spec's CAN is defined as 'able, or possible in fact'.
items.example: la verba ka'e sanga 'the child can sing (is the kind of thing that can)' vs pu'i 'can and has'
items.how_now: CAN fail THEME test -- 'the test is able to fail', 'it sometimes fails', or 'failure is not ruled out'? (POSSIBLE is reserved for the writer's own doubt)
items.suggestion: Clarify: CAN = the world allows it (ability or circumstance); 'it happens on some occasions' is SOMETIMES; 'for all I know' is POSSIBLE. Demonstrated vs untested ability is CAN plus a second clause, no new particle.

items.what: Lojban's elidable terminators (ku, vau, ke'e), left-grouping defaults and the bo override are what learners get wrong even though the grammar is formally unambiguous; the spec's always-written ( ) { } and 'all modifiers attach to the head' avoid this.
items.example: lo barda tcadu gerku '(big city) dog' vs barda gerku bo tcadu; 'ba ku le nunsalci' vs 'ba le nunsalci' change meaning by one elided word
items.how_now: error KIND network KIND (VERY slow) -- flat attachment, explicit brackets
items.suggestion: Keep as is and write it down as a commitment: no elidable closers, no precedence between particles, ever. Copy Lojban's good half instead: a machine-tested grammar (run the EBNF through a parser generator to prove it has no ambiguities such as the AND one above).

items.category: mention vs use of native text
items.what: Lojban has separate quotes for a single word (zo), grammatical Lojban text (lu ... li'u) and foreign text (zoi); the spec has « » for foreign text and BY blocks for speech, but nothing for talking about a native word or particle as a word.
items.example: zo klama 'the word klama'
items.how_now: DEFINE covers introducing a term; 'the root X is ambiguous' or 'you wrote MUST where SHOULD was meant' has no approved form (a bare block is a proposition, not a string)
items.suggestion: Rule: native material mentioned as text goes in « » after a class head (word KIND «...»), same as foreign text; the decoder then never tries to parse it.

items.what: Ithkuil makes some twenty categories with up to 96 values each obligatory on every word, and even its author says a word takes much more thought to produce; its failure is choice cost, not expressive power.
items.example: 9 configurations x 4 affiliations x 4 perspectives x 6 extensions on every noun; 9 sanctions, 6 validations, 32 aspects, 24 biases on verbs
items.how_now: everything optional except the opener (13 values); aspect list already has 14 members with overlaps (HABIT/OFTEN/ALWAYS, DONE/ALREADY/PAST)
items.suggestion: Adopt a rule for every closed list: each member must be choosable by a one-line test against its neighbours, and every list has a stated unmarked reading. Say explicitly that CLAIM is the fallback opener when the others are unclear. Reject new particles that only split an existing one.

items.what: Ithkuil's 24 Bias values (and Lojban's attitudinals) include hope, apprehension, approval and disapproval; the spec's nine attitudes cover reactions to facts (GLAD, REGRET, ANNOYED, SURPRISE) but none toward an open outcome.
items.example: 'Hopefully this fixes it.' / 'I am afraid the data is lost.'
items.how_now: PLAN GLAD POSSIBLE fix ... ? (GLAD + POSSIBLE is a guess at 'hopefully'); or CLAIM hope AGENT ME THEME { ... } which loses the attitude slot
items.suggestion: Add HOPE and WORRY to the attitude list (attitude slot, also focus slot before a phrase). They are the two that reasoning and status reports use constantly.

items.what: Ithkuil's Context and Essence categories mark whether a word is meant existentially, functionally or as a symbol/representation; the spec has IRONY and JEST for whole utterances but nothing that flags one phrase as not literal.
items.example: 'the heart of the algorithm', 'a bottleneck', 'the test is flaky'
items.how_now: heart OF algorithm (decoder and reader cannot tell organ from core); THAN heart gives simile only as a clause role
items.suggestion: Either add FIGURE to the focus slot (FIGURE heart OF algorithm), or rule that metaphor is forbidden and must be written as THAN-likeness or the literal root (centre). With compositional compounds the second is safer; decide and state it.

items.what: Ithkuil derives complementary concepts from one root by stem pattern (parent/child from 'family member', and similar buy/sell, give/take pairs), cutting the root count.
items.example: omm- 'parent' / amm- 'child' from one root mm- 'nuclear family member'
items.how_now: sell AGENT A THEME x TO B vs buy AGENT B THEME x FROM A -- two roots for one event; give/receive, teach/learn, lend/borrow likewise
items.suggestion: Since roles are tagged and order is free, keep one root per event (trade, give, teach) and let AGENT/TO/FROM choose the viewpoint; list the dropped converses in the lexicon as aliases the validator rewrites.

items.what: Ithkuil keeps Illocution (assert, ask, command), Validation (evidence) and Sanction (how to take it: allegation, axiom, refutation) as three independent categories; the spec folds evidence and speech act into the single opener.
items.example: an axiomatic rule that is recalled, not enacted; a request that follows from earlier steps
items.how_now: RULE MUST ... = laid down here; reporting an existing law or standard: RECALLED MUST ... ? or RULE ... with BY? Likewise quoting vs making a definition.
items.suggestion: Clarify: RULE and DEFINE are only for enacting in this text; an existing rule or definition is reported with an evidence opener plus MUST/DEFINE-free wording (RECALLED MUST ... FROM standard). One line in Clarifications.

items.what: Toki Pona builds everything from compounds, but their meanings are either vague or silently conventional (jan pona 'friend', telo nasa 'alcohol'), and different speakers describe the same thing differently.
items.example: pana e sona 'give knowledge' = teach; laso loje vs loje laso
items.how_now: store KIND data = database (spec's own example); another writer: collection KIND data, system KIND (store THEME data); the decoder cannot map either back to 'database'
items.suggestion: Add a compound registry beside the root lexicon: an approved compound has one form and one English rendering, goes through validate.py, and anything unregistered must be introduced with DEFINE at first use in a text.

items.what: Toki Pona roots are deliberately polysemous (suli = big, long, important), which makes it unusable for exact exposition; the spec has the opposite defect of assuming every English content word is a root, so it inherits English synonymy and polysemy.
items.example: suli 'big / tall / important'; English run (a race, a program), light, right, charge
items.how_now: big / large / huge, begin / start, error / fault / bug / mistake are all 'roots'; run AGENT A and run THEME program use two senses of one root
items.suggestion: Fix a finite root list with one sense per root and an alias table from English near-synonyms; a second sense must be a different root or a registered compound. This is the precondition for every 'small root list' idea below.

items.what: Proper names never stand alone; they modify a class word, so the reader always knows what kind of thing is named.
items.example: jan Lisa 'person Lisa', ma Kanata 'land Canada'
items.how_now: name«Paris» (person, city or model?)
items.suggestion: Recommend, not require: class head + KIND + name on first mention (city KIND name«Paris»), bare name afterwards or a handle. No new particle.

items.what: Hawaiian has a dedicated pattern for 'A is at B' (Aia A ma B), separate from 'A is a B' (He B A) and 'A is identical to B' ('O A B); the spec defines the last two but not the first.
items.example: Aia 'o Mary ma Hilo 'Mary is in Hilo'; Aia 'o ia maloko o ka wai 'it is inside the water'
items.how_now: (inside REL box) THEME X ? / exist THEME X AT inside REL box ? / stay ... ? ('there is no is'; no approved form for being somewhere)
items.suggestion: Rule: location is predicated with the relational root or place as predicate in ( ): (inside REL box) THEME X, (AT city) not allowed. Add one example to the spec; do the same for time ('the meeting is before lunch').

items.what: Hawaiian marks perfective (ua), progressive (e ... ana) and intentive rather than past/present/future; a completed event needs no tense at all.
items.example: ua hana au 'I worked / I have worked'
items.how_now: the spec's own examples vary: PAST change AGENT YOU THEME S (2) but ASK DONE send THEME release; a third writer would put PAST DONE
items.suggestion: Rule: PAST places the event before now and says nothing about its result; DONE says the result holds at the reference time and implies nothing else; never write both unless both are meant. Give the one-line test ('is the present state the point?' -> DONE).

items.what: Hawaiian (like Guarani, Aymara and Ainu) has separate words for 'we including you' and 'we excluding you'.
items.example: kaua 'you and I' vs maua 'I and another, not you'
items.how_now: inclusive: ME AND YOU (works); exclusive: US leaves it open, and there is no phrase-level 'except you' (EXCEPT is a clause role)
items.suggestion: Rule, no particle: US always excludes the addressee; inclusive is US AND YOU or ME AND YOU. This reverses the current 'US says nothing' clarification and costs nothing.

items.what: Hawaiian possessives split into a-class (the possessor controls or created the relation) and o-class (not controlled: body, house, name); Nahuatl similarly marks part-of-the-body possession apart from ownership.
items.example: Nahuatl nonac 'my meat (to eat)' vs nonacayo 'my flesh'
items.how_now: OF is 'owner or whole'; report OF Ana (owns? wrote? is about?), bug OF Ana (reported? caused? assigned?), team OF Ana (owns or belongs to?)
items.suggestion: Rule: OF is strictly ownership or part-whole; authorship, membership, assignment and the like must use a clause modifier (report KIND { write AGENT Ana THEME SELF }). Consider a short approved list of 2-3 such patterns.

items.what: Post-verbal particles mark motion or orientation toward the speaker, away, up or down on any verb (mai, aku, a'e, iho); Nahuatl (on-/hual-) and Thai (ma/pai after the verb) do the same.
items.example: verb + mai 'hither', verb + aku 'away'; Thai khao ma 'enter come' = come in
items.how_now: move AGENT A TO ME / FROM ME; come and go as separate roots
items.suggestion: Leave out: a written reasoning medium has almost no shared physical viewpoint. Rule that come/go/bring/take are not roots (move TO / FROM, carry TO / FROM), which also shrinks the root list.

items.what: Hawaiian and Lakota both have near-speaker, near-addressee and distant demonstratives plus a separate 'the aforementioned' series; the spec has THIS (present/pointed at) and THAT (already identified) only.
items.example: keia / kena / kela; ua ... nei 'the aforementioned'; Lakota k'un 'the (previously mentioned)'
items.how_now: THIS file (here), THAT file (mentioned before); 'that one over there, not yet mentioned', 'the one on your side', 'the following' have no form (the last is STEP + later label)
items.suggestion: Keep two terms but state that THAT is purely anaphoric and never spatial, and that anything forward-pointing uses a label. Distal deixis: leave out.

items.what: Lakota enclitics mark reported information (keye 'they say', skhe 'I understand') apart from plain assertion; Nahuatl quil and Lojban ti'e do the same, and Aymara splits tenses by personal vs non-personal knowledge.
items.example: yapi keye 'they went, they say'
items.how_now: GIVEN covers a document, a tool, another party's say-so and the writer's own observation alike; say AGENT A THEME { ... } reports the saying but hides whether the writer accepts it
items.suggestion: Split GIVEN by adding one opener TOLD (a person or document says so; writer passes it on without having checked), keeping GIVEN for what the writer itself observed or was shown by a tool. A FROM phrase names the source. For a model, user-says vs tool-shows vs I-ran-it is the distinction that most affects trust.

items.what: Lakota (and Guarani) mark the sole participant of a verb as actor-like or undergoer-like depending on whether it controls the event.
items.example: active wa- 'I (do)' vs stative ma- 'I (am / undergo)'
items.how_now: fail THEME test (example 1) but arrive AGENT A (spec); die / fall / sleep / wait / exist: AGENT or THEME? States are AGENT by clarification (know, see), processes unclear
items.suggestion: One rule: the sole participant is AGENT only if it controls or instigates the event, otherwise THEME. Then fall AGENT A = on purpose and fall THEME A = by accident, for free. Reconcile with the 'experiencer is AGENT' clarification (it is the exception; list its roots).

items.what: Lakota has distinct question enclitics for an ordinary question, a rhetorical or oratorical one (hunwo), and a dubitative one where the hearer is not expected to know (so/se, wan).
items.example: seca wan 'can it be as it seems?' (wondering, no answer demanded)
items.how_now: ASK ... for all three; ASK YES/NO only marks the expected answer; a model 'thinking aloud' and a model needing the user's reply look the same
items.suggestion: Rule: ASK with CALL or a YOU role is put to the addressee and expects ANSWER; ASK with neither is an open question the writer poses to itself. Rhetorical = ASK YES/NO CERTAIN. No new particle, but it must be written down.

items.what: Lakota has two indefinite articles: wan for a real, particular one and wanzi for a hypothetical or not-yet-existing one; Lojban le/lo and Thai classifier order ('glass CL one' vs 'glass one CL') make related cuts.
items.example: 'I am looking for a horse' (a particular one / any horse)
items.how_now: seek AGENT ME THEME SOME file vs THEME ANY file -- plausible, but SOME is not defined as specific and a bare head says nothing
items.suggestion: Rule: SOME = at least one exists, identity open; ANY = whichever, need not exist; a particular one the writer has in mind is introduced with NAMED (binding a handle asserts a specific referent). No new particle.

items.what: Nahuatl obligatorily distinguishes a known-but-unmentioned object (null anaphora) from a nonspecific one (te- 'people', tla- 'things') and from an impersonal with no agent in mind; Guarani antipassive (poro-, mba'e-) and middle (je-) do the same.
items.example: nitlacua 'I eat (something)' vs niccua 'I eat it'; tlacuilo 'there is taking'; Guarani amba'ejogua 'I am shopping'
items.how_now: PAST open THEME door -- someone opened it, it opened by itself, or the opener is the one we were just talking about?
items.suggestion: Rule: an omitted role is unspecified and never anaphoric (use a handle or THAT to refer back); 'by itself, no agent' is AGENT NONE; 'people in general' is AGENT GENERIC person. Three lines in Clarifications remove the largest source of decoder guessing.

items.what: Nahuatl has an optative for wishes (ma ...), a past optative for unfulfillable wishes ('if only') and an admonitive that warns something bad may happen ('beware lest').
items.example: ma nicchihua 'may I do it'; In tla tinocniuh xiyeni 'if only you were my friend'; admonitive 'watch out or you will fall'
items.how_now: REQUEST with no addressee is already 'procedure step'; CLAIM want AGENT ME THEME { ... } states a desire instead of wishing; warning: REQUEST careful ... FOR { NOT fall }
items.suggestion: With HOPE and WORRY as attitudes (see Ithkuil item) no new opener is needed: wish = CLAIM HOPE ..., 'if only' = CLAIM HOPE UNREAL ..., warning = CLAIM WORRY POSSIBLE ... or REQUEST ... EXCEPT. Bless these three forms.

items.what: Nahuatl derives 'one who does', 'one who habitually does', 'thing done' and 'thing done with' directly from a verb, and the adjunctor in turns any clause into 'the one who ...' with no head noun.
items.example: in cuica 'the one who sings'; tlahtoani 'one who speaks (customarily), ruler'; in tlein ticnequiz 'whatever you want'
items.how_now: person KIND { sing AGENT SELF } ; ANY thing KIND { want AGENT YOU THEME SELF } -- a dummy head, KIND, braces and SELF for every 'singer', 'the sender', 'what you want'
items.suggestion: Allow a role particle directly before a root inside a phrase head as shorthand: (AGENT sing) = the one who sings, (THEME want AGENT YOU) = what you want, (WITH cut) = cutting tool. It reuses existing particles and the ( ) rule.

items.what: An incorporated generic object or modifier turns an event with a participant into a named kind of activity, distinct from the same verb with a specific object.
items.example: nicchihua cactli 'I make shoes' vs nicacchihua 'I shoe-make'; xochicueponi 'it flower-blossoms (blossoms like a flower)'
items.how_now: make AGENT A THEME GENERIC shoe vs (make KIND shoe) AGENT A -- both legal; the second is exactly incorporation
items.suggestion: Bless (root KIND root) as the activity-type predicate and say when to prefer it (occupations, habits, compound verbs like bug-fix); it gives compound verbs without new roots.

items.what: Guarani puts past and future on nouns: former, future/intended, and 'was going to be but never was'.
items.example: teta ruvichakue 'ex-president', teta ruvichara 'president-elect'
items.how_now: person KIND { PAST (president) THEME SELF } ; 'the previous value', 'the future owner', 'my then manager' all need a clause, because time particles only stand before a predicate
items.suggestion: Allow a time particle in the unit's pre-head slot beside focus/strength: PAST president, FUTURE owner, UNREAL FUTURE husband. (POSSIBLE bug for 'alleged bug' already works this way.)

items.what: The suffix -ra'e marks that the speaker doubted or believed otherwise before and has now found out ('so it was X after all').
items.example: Nde rejoguara'e petei ta'angambyry pyahu 'so you did buy a new television after all'
items.how_now: SURPRISE marks the feeling; REBUT is for the addressee's belief; CONTRAST 4 says step 4 differs but not that step 4 is withdrawn
items.suggestion: Add a relation CORRECT label: this sentence replaces the target, which the writer no longer holds. Reasoning text needs retraction more than almost any other relation, and a decoder can then strike the earlier step.

items.what: Guarani -se 'want to' (like Nahuatl -nequi, Toki Pona preverbs, Thai auxiliaries) attaches to the verb and shares its subject; a different-subject wish needs a full clause.
items.example: (Che) anemoaranduse 'I want to study'; Nahuatl niquittaznequi 'I want to see it'
items.how_now: want AGENT ME THEME { study AGENT ME } ; try AGENT A THEME { open AGENT A THEME door } -- agent written twice, or left out and then 'unspecified'
items.suggestion: Add WANT and TRY to the modal slot (the agent's own will / attempt): WANT study AGENT ME; PAST TRY open AGENT A THEME door; NOT WANT / WANT NOT fall out of the existing scope rule. Different-subject wishes keep the want + block form.

items.what: Guarani derives 'make X happen' from intransitives with mbo- and 'have someone do it' from transitives with -uka, so kill/teach/bring-closer need no roots of their own.
items.example: amboguata kure 'I make the pig walk'; mbokatupyry 'make skilled' = teach; moagui 'make near' = bring closer
items.how_now: walk AGENT pig CAUSE ME ? / cause AGENT ME THEME { walk AGENT pig } ? / break AGENT ME THEME cup (works because break is labile) ; big AGENT ME THEME file = enlarge?
items.suggestion: Rule: adding AGENT to a root whose sole participant is THEME gives the direct causative (die THEME x -> die AGENT a THEME x = kill; big AGENT a THEME x = enlarge); causing someone else to act is cause/let + block; CAUSE role is for reasons and non-agent causes. Then kill, raise, drop, enlarge, show leave the root list.

items.what: Ainu has a separate person form for 'one / people in general', also used for inclusive we and as a polite 'you'.
items.example: a- / -an 'one, people' as subject marker
items.how_now: ANY person = 'one' (spec); 'people say', 'it is known that', 'you never know': AGENT ANY person? AGENT GENERIC person? omit AGENT?
items.suggestion: Rule: generic human agent = GENERIC person (typical people), ANY person = whoever it may be (rules, permissions), omitted AGENT = unspecified. Polite 'you' is POLITE in the focus slot before YOU, which the grammar already allows.

items.what: Ainu has a closed class of plural verbs marking that the event itself is multiple (many acts or many participants each acting); Yimas reduplicates the verb for repeated action and Ithkuil has nine Phase values for it.
items.example: Yimas ya-n-arkark-... 'he repeatedly broke them'; 'knocked (several raps)' vs 'knocked (once)'
items.how_now: AGAIN = once more; OFTEN / HABIT = over a long period; 'kept clicking', 'retried over and over within one run' fits none clearly; ONGOING click?
items.suggestion: With the proposed TIMES particle: MANY TIMES click = repeated within one occasion; keep OFTEN/HABIT for recurrence across occasions. State the contrast in the aspect list.

items.category: what a small verb inventory costs
items.what: Kalam expresses most verb meanings with a small closed set of general verbs strung in fixed sequences; the sequences are conventional and have to be learned as units just as words are.
items.example: d ap 'get come' = bring; d am 'get go' = take; am d ap 'go get come' = fetch; nb nn 'eat perceive' = taste; d nn 'touch perceive' = feel
items.how_now: the spec assumes every English content word is a root, so no cost yet; with a small list, 'fetch' becomes a three-root expression every writer must build identically
items.suggestion: A small root list does not shrink the lexicon, it moves it into multi-root expressions. Budget for it: (1) the compound registry, (2) one fixed composition pattern (next item), (3) a decoder table from registered combinations to single English words. Kalam shows roughly a hundred verb roots suffice only with a large stock of memorised combinations.

items.what: Kalam builds transitive verbs as action + resulting state in one clause with shared participants, and negation or failure can target the result alone (as in Thai 'listen not understand').
items.example: pak wk 'strike shattered' = smash; pug sug 'blow extinguished' = blow out; tb tk 'cut sever' = cut off
items.how_now: (strike KIND shatter) THEME cup ? (shatter KIND strike) ? strike THEME cup TO shatter ? two clauses with RESULT ? 'so hot that it melted', 'painted it red', 'hammered it flat' have no approved form
items.suggestion: Rule: the end state of the THEME goes in TO as a root or block (strike THEME cup TO shatter; paint THEME door TO red; NOT before the TO phrase = tried without the result). Manner or means goes in WITH or KIND. Extend TO's definition from 'recipient or end point' to 'end point or resulting state'.

items.what: Kalam has no separate roots for bring/take/fetch (get + come/go) and uses one 'perceive' verb with a sense-organ or contact verb for see, hear, feel, taste, smell.
items.example: am d ap 'go get come'; nb nn 'eat perceive' = taste
items.how_now: bring / take / fetch / carry / send / deliver and see / hear / feel / taste / smell / notice are all separate assumed roots
items.suggestion: Decide the decomposition once and list the English verbs that are NOT roots: carry + TO/FROM for bring/take; perceive WITH eye/ear/tongue only if see/hear are really to be dropped (keep know and think as roots: merging them, as Kalam does, would hurt reasoning text).

items.what: Thai time and aspect markers are optional and an unmarked verb is simply unspecified (chan kin thi nan = I eat / am eating / ate / will eat there); Lojban is the same by design.
items.example: chan kin thi nan
items.how_now: spec: 'unmarked = timeless', yet example 1 GIVEN fail THEME test KIND login is decoded as a present fact; writers who simply omit time will be read as claiming a timeless truth
items.suggestion: Change the rule: unmarked = time not stated (taken from the default set by the header or context); a law-like, timeless statement is marked by GENERIC on the phrase or ALWAYS. An omission should never carry a strong claim.

items.what: Thai laeo after a state marks that the situation is new ('I am hungry now, I was not before'); Nahuatl ye does the same and oc marks the opposite, no change.
items.example: chan hio laeo 'I am hungry now / I have become hungry'
items.how_now: 'It works now', 'the file became large': BEGIN work ? NOW work ? ALREADY work ? MORE big ? (STILL and NOT STILL cover the no-change and stopped cases)
items.suggestion: Rule: BEGIN before a state means 'come to be so' (BEGIN big = become big; DONE BEGIN work = works now, did not before). NOW is only 'at present, may change'. Add 'become' to the list of words that are not roots.

items.what: Thai khoei marks that something has happened at least once in one's experience, separate from past and perfect.
items.example: khao khoei pai 'he has been (there) before'
items.how_now: ASK PAST SOMETIMES see AGENT YOU THEME error ? ASK NOT NEVER ... ? (NEVER exists, its positive partner does not)
items.suggestion: With TIMES: ATLEAST 1 TIMES = ever, and NEVER stays as its negation; or add EVER to the aspect list and define NEVER as NOT EVER. Pick one.

items.what: Thai forms the superlative with thi sut 'to the end / of all', and the comparison set is a separate phrase; the spec has MOST and LEAST but no stated place for the set compared.
items.example: khao uan thi sut 'he is the fattest (of all)'
items.how_now: MOST fast THEME X THAN ALL method ? ... ABOUT 3 method ? ... OF ... ? (THAN is defined only for MORE/LESS/EQUAL)
items.suggestion: Rule: after MOST/LEAST the THAN phrase names the set compared (MOST fast THEME X THAN ALL 3 method); without THAN the set is contextual.

items.category: beneficiary vs purpose in one clause
items.what: Thai marks the beneficiary with hai ('give') after the verb while purpose is a following verb, so both can appear together; the adversative passive (thuk) additionally marks that the subject is negatively affected.
items.example: khao an nangsue hai 'he reads the book for (us)'; khao thuk ti 'he got hit (suffered it)'
items.how_now: FOR is both purpose and beneficiary and a role appears once per clause: 'wrote a script for Ana for testing' -> FOR (Ana AND { test }) mixes two meanings; 'it crashed on me' has only REGRET
items.suggestion: Rule: FOR with a person or group = beneficiary, FOR with a block or event root = purpose, and both may be given as FOR (A AND { ... }) with that reading fixed; or move beneficiary to TO. Negatively affected party: leave out (use a second clause with harm).

items.what: Thai requires a classifier or measure word between number and noun, which makes 'two bottles of beer' and 'two beers' the same construction and keeps counting units explicit.
items.example: bia song khuat 'beer two bottle'; khru ha khon 'teacher five person'
items.how_now: 2 bottle KIND beer (KIND covers content) ; 3 «kg» KIND rice ? rice SPAN 3 «kg» ? 3 «kg» rice ? ('a unit may follow a number' but the link to the substance is not shown)
items.suggestion: Rule and one example: measured amounts are number + unit as head, substance after KIND (3 «kg» KIND rice, 2 bottle KIND beer); SPAN is only for the extent of a predicate (weigh THEME x SPAN 3 «kg»).

items.what: Aymara has verbal suffixes that reverse an action or give the opposite of the root's meaning, so opposites are derived rather than listed.
items.example: multiplier/reverser suffixes: root 'tie' -> 'untie'
items.how_now: NOT big (merely not big) vs small (separate root); do vs undo, load vs unload, lock vs unlock as separate roots
items.suggestion: Add OPPOSITE to the degree slot (OPPOSITE big = small, OPPOSITE lock = unlock), distinct from NOT. It removes about a third of adjective and many verb roots and the decoder maps the registered pairs back to single English words.

items.what: Aymara's obligatory split between personal-knowledge and non-personal-knowledge forms, plus its verbal comparative -jama ('as if, seemingly'), marks a statement as the speaker's inference without listing premises.
items.example: 'It seems the server is down' (inferred from symptoms, not seen and not reasoned from stated steps)
items.how_now: DERIVED is 'followed by the labels it rests on'; with no labels to cite: DERIVED LIKELY ... ? CLAIM LIKELY ... ? seem THEME { ... } ?
items.suggestion: Clarify that DERIVED with no labels means 'inferred from evidence not written down', and that seem/appear are not roots. That gives the classic three-way evidential set (GIVEN seen, TOLD reported, DERIVED inferred) with RECALLED for memory.

items.category: sequence vs simultaneity inside a sentence
items.what: Yimas joins verbs in one word either bare (simultaneous or causally linked) or with -mpi (one after the other), sharing all participants.
items.example: kulanan-kanta 'walk-follow' = walking while following; ak-mpi-wul 'push, then put down'
items.how_now: (rise AND walk) AGENT A gives no order and no separate time/aspect; rise AGENT A AND walk AGENT A repeats the agent and AND says nothing about order; SEQUENCE works only between sentences
items.suggestion: Allow the relation words as clause joiners inside a body: clause SEQUENCE clause (then), and rule that a later clause with no AGENT in such a chain shares the first clause's AGENT. Simultaneity stays WHEN { ... }.

items.what: Yimas tracks participants through ten noun classes cross-referenced on the verb, so 'it' is rarely ambiguous; the spec's handles are the unambiguous equivalent but must be planned at first mention.
items.example: krayn narman k-n-tay 'frog(VI) woman(II) VI.O-3SG.A-see' = the woman saw the frog
items.how_now: bare THAT = 'the one already identified' -- which one, when two things were mentioned? THAT + root (THAT frog) works; a handle works only if NAMED was written earlier
items.suggestion: Rule: bare THAT refers to the previous sentence as a whole or its THEME, nothing else; any other back-reference repeats the head root (THAT frog) or uses a handle. Allow late binding: THAT frog NAMED F.

items.what: Yimas has four pasts (today, yesterday, a few days ago, long ago) and two futures (tomorrow, later); Kalam has a similar set.
items.example: wa-t 'went today', wa-nan 'went yesterday', wa-kiantut 'a few days ago', wa-ntut 'long ago'
items.how_now: PAST NEAR / PAST / PAST FAR; no stated boundary, so 'yesterday' may be NEAR for one writer and plain for another
items.suggestion: Leave the three steps; state that NEAR and FAR are relative to the timescale of the text and that anything that matters is given by a WHEN phrase. No new particles.
